title: Everything New In Wardogs Season 2
description: Wardogs is about to get shaken up with Season 2. The tactical shooter will get a fresh arsenal, new vehicles, a round of balance changes, and more ways to fortify the battlefield. The update will be available at 9:30 AM UTC on October 15, with the community already discussing its potential impact. Some players have been enthusiastic about the scale of the changes, although the new economy and logistics adjustments have raised concerns among players who rely more heavily on those systems. Here are the 10 changes that will have the biggest impact on Wardogs, followed by everything new in Wardogs Season 2. Blue Team Bribery Wardogs is trying something unusual to solve a problem money alone can't usually fix: bribing players to choose the team they don't want to play. Lonestar--or the blue team--has struggled with lower win rates and earned itself quite the reputation as the cursed faction in the game. Bulkhead says that could be down to uniform visibility or spawn locations, but weird player superstitions are probably the real reason people avoid the team. Season 2 introduces extra cash and XP for Lonestar victories, plus additional rewards for certain teamplay actions. Players on any faction that's at least 40 points behind the team in second place will also receive a 20% vendor discount to encourage them to equip their best loadouts and try to recoup the loss. This is being treated as a Season 2 experiment rather than a permanent balance solution, but it remains to be seen whether the rewards are enough to change players' preference. Four New Weapons Season 2 adds four new weapons, giving players more options across multiple combat roles: TCX-SPR: An assault rifle chambered in 7.62x39mm. PP-19 Bizon: A 9x19mm submachine gun. Evo-3 Ultra: A.308 Winchester light machine gun. M14: A.308 Winchester marksman rifle. The new weapons arrive alongside additional optics, magazines, muzzles, and bipods. They also tie into the revised progression system, so players will have…

title: A Sentient Snowman Is (Surprisingly) My Favorite Part Of This RPG Remake
description: At this year's New York Comic Con, I met with Square Enix to check out two of its upcoming RPG projects. One was Final Fantasy VII Revelation, a game firmly planted in the modern era of video games with top-of-the-line visuals and all the trimmings of a AAA, big-budget game. The other was Romancing Saga 3: Destinies United, a remake of a classic turn-based RPG from the mid-1990s. At first glance, the remake's updated visuals and faster gameplay are easily apparent draws for newer players, but that doesn't change that this game is built around the core of the original Romancing Saga 3, an RPG that calls back to a bygone era for the genre. Remaking a classic like this is a balancing act, but based on my brief time playing the game, it seems like Square Enix is on track to unite the best aspects of the two wildly different eras of RPGs. Flurry the snowman A Flurry of action The demo takes place in Gwayne's Den, the home of a massive dragon terrorizing the nearby Louv Peninsula. I take control of party leader Khalid and head down the mountain path, where I spot an enemy not paying attention to my approach. By sneaking up to the foe and pressing X, I can stealthily swing my sword at it, and, if I connect, I launch a Preemptive Strike--this starts the ensuing battle with every enemy having lost a bit of their hit points. It's not a massive chunk of health, so I didn't feel too bad if the enemy proved difficult to sneak up on, but the head start always felt good when I did pull it off. Battles play out in classic turn-based style, with a turn-order indicator situated at the top of the screen. Most of my party is ready for battle, with leader Khalid, fairy Peony, fighter Ellen, and masked swordsman Robin sporting a full kit of weapons and abilities. There's a fifth party member, Flurry the actual snowman, who's underpowered compared to the rest, but it still packs a wallop with its punches. Also, just to make clear what I said just now: Yes, Flurry is an honest-to-goodness…

title: Epic Is Overhauling Its Anti-Cheat So That Fortnite Can Finally Come To A New Platform
description: Thanks to devices such as the Steam Deck and Steam Machine, as well as the ongoing issues with Windows, gaming on Linux looks a lot more attractive over the last few years. Its biggest hurdle is still multiplayer games and their anti-cheat systems, but Epic Games is committed to bringing one of the biggest around to the operating system soon. Epic Games has announced that it is working on a Linux version for Fortnite. It's going to act as a test for Epic's overhaul of EAC (Easy Anti-Cheat), its solution to those developing multiplayer games in Unreal Engine to prevent cheating (most recently used in Gears of War: E-Day). Epic says that it has offered Linux support for its current version of EAC, but that most developers (itself included) opted not to use it and instead omit Linux support entirely because of its inability to be as protective as its Windows version. A native rebuild of EAC, that doesn't require translation layers such as Proton, would help Epic bring the software up to par with Windows, at which point it would be comfortable finally releasing a native Linux version of Fortnite. In a blog post, Epic says that once it has reached this stage, it will make this available to other developers, too. "We are also planning to pilot EAC Linux v2 in Fortnite first, where we’ll test it in a live environment and refine it based on what we learn. Once we’ve validated EAC v2’s effectiveness, we’ll make it available to more game developers so they can bring their multiplayer games to Linux players too." Epic hasn't shared a timeline for when it expects Fortnite on Linux, but does say that its pilot program will be available through its new Epic Game Store launcher. Announced at the same time, Epic has decided to follow through with its commitment to AI-developed software earlier this week, with the new launcher labelled as "vibe coded" because "programming is hard". This version is still in preview and lacks all of the features currently on the main version of the…

title: Xbox Survey About Exclusives Includes A Nuclear Strategy, But Wait Just A Minute
description: Microsoft is reportedly surveying a subset of Xbox users about changing its plans for exclusive games going forward--possibly in a big way--and that's no surprise given Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has alluded to changes to the exclusivity strategy in the future. At the same time, a survey like this is not necessarily indicative of anything beyond Microsoft conducting research. After all, there is an entire team at Xbox called Xbox Research that... researches all manner of things, and the results of that research doesn't always lead to changes in the marketplace. Windows Central reports that a new survey was issued to some Xbox Insiders this week, and the site confirmed the survey to be real. The survey asks how members might feel about the totally nuclear option of making all Xbox-developed games except Call of Duty exclusive to Xbox on console. "Imagine it was announced that all future title releases from every Xbox-developed gaming franchise except Call of Duty will be console-exclusive to Xbox," the survey asks. It goes on: "For Minecraft only, existing titles would no longer be available for purchase on PlayStation or Nintendo consoles and would not receive any new content updates. However, there is no impact to any of the existing titles or content you already own. Nothing changes on PC with this announcement." The survey asks respondents to say in this scenario, where they would be most likely to play any of the exclusive content. The choices are: On an existing Xbox I own On a new Xbox Series X|S I would decide to purchase On a PC I would skip playing because it would now be unavailable on my preferred console Something else Not interested in playing the exclusive content Another page of the survey specifically asks about Fallout, polling users about how they would feel if future Fallout games would be console-exclusive to Xbox, and with nothing changing at all on PC. Windows Central reported that the survey also asked these same questions about The Elder Scrolls,…

title: GTA 6 Reviews: When They Could Be Released
description: Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 releases on November 19, but when will you be able to read reviews? According to historical precedent and a new report, reviews for the open-world crime game should be available before launch. Insider Gaming reported that reviews for GTA 6 will be posted at some point before November 19, but the exact timing is unknown for now. According to insider NateTheHate, Rockstar will send copies of GTA 6 to reviewers before the end of October, so any time now, seemingly. A scene from GTA 6. What history tells us The last GTA game, GTA 5, was released on September 17, 2013, and reviews for the game were published starting on September 16. For Rockstar's next game, 2018's Red Dead Redemption II, reviews also went live one day prior to release. This doesn't necessarily mean Rockstar will follow the same playbook for GTA 6, however. Nothing is confirmed at this stage. GTA 6 launches on November 19-- unless it's delayed again --for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. It's expected to be the biggest game of 2026 and maybe all time, and it's reportedly on pace to earn $2 billion in revenue before launch. A lot of new details about GTA 6 recently came to light, including how the game originally had a bigger scope and could have launched sooner, Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick’s response to a big delay, and the absurd amount of detail in the game. We also learned that GTA 6 did not in fact cost $1.5 billion to make and that an entire studio was spun up to create NPCs. Rockstar also discussed how its GTA 6 realism experiment began with beer and sandwiches and that the studio says it won’t need another eight years to release its next game. Beyond all of this, Rockstar reacted to the game's high-profile hack in 2022.

title: I’m Enjoying Fire Emblem More By Not Playing Fire Emblem More
description: Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave has some of the best tactical gameplay in the series to date, but actually digging into the art of seeing units bonk each other on the head in turn-based combat is a massive slog. Between a shift to Persona-like storytelling and a laundry list of chores, the game can feel like the equivalent of the Achilles and the tortoise paradox ( via a Jujutsu Kaisen breakdown ), because the closer I get to actually moving the story forward, the further I feel I am from actually engaging in some of that fantastic warfare. And that's a shame, because Fortune's Weave is a really great evolution of the core Fire Emblem gameplay experience. The tactics game has more nuance to its rock-paper-nuns-with-guns formula in this entry, the jobs system offers more variety, and the unique tools at each Flame Lord's disposal make each one a force to be reckoned with. So what's the solution to enjoying the best parts of Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave, without getting bogged down by all the busywork in between? It turns out that if you want to enjoy Fire Emblem more, you may need to play less of it. Don't sweat the training One thing I've discovered is a gameplay loop that Fire Emblem expects you to follow with each Flame Lord. Each of the main chapters is squeezed into lengthy moments of downtime, where you're free to explore to your heart's content--or within the limits of your renown and overall standing in the countryside beyond. Options include dungeon-diving, visiting gods for favors, taking training courses, mining for materials, taking on odd jobs, recruiting new members to your team, and so on. I'm busy skipping most of that as I dive into the game's later chapters. Sure, improving your stats with combat training outside of the arena is a great way to unlock new skills, but there's a ceiling to just how you can improve. Going from E-rank to C-rank is reasonably quick, but once you hit those higher levels, progress slows to a crawl, even when you unlock higher…

title: Retro Handhelds Loaded With Unlicensed Games Could Face Government Crackdown
description: The Electronic Software Association (ESA) has a serious bone to pick with retro handhelds that are packaged with tons of unlicensed pre-installed, calling these devices "superfakes" that should face some sort of suppression by the US government. According to an October 6 filing with the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR)--which monitors marketplaces that are accused of engaging in or enabling piracy and counterfeiting--the ESA is urging the government to clamp down on what it calls "illicit plug-and-play consoles and handheld devices." The ESA wants the USTR to add these emulation devices to the Notorious Markets List, the agency's annual report identifying which markets are participating in such behavior, thereby barring or slowing their profits. "In the video game sector, illicit plug-and-play consoles and handheld devices are the functional equivalent of superfakes," the ESA told the USTR. "They can look and feel like legitimate, mass-market consumer electronics: molded housings, color displays, polished user interfaces, retail packaging, product reviews, warranty-like representations, and listings on familiar e-commerce platforms. Yet their commercial appeal rests solely on a concealed memory card or internal drive loaded with hundreds, thousands, or even tens of thousands of unauthorized copies of copyright-protected games." The ESA puts a specific spotlight on Anbernic, a console manufacturer that sells 3DS- and Game Boy-looking devices packed with thousands of games from systems like the NES and SNES to the PlayStation 1 and Sega Genesis. Though maybe the most prominent example, another one that comes to mind is rapper Soulja Boy's various console attempts. The filing also targets digital marketplaces that it says distribute or sell modded accounts and pirated games such as Eldorado, FunPay, G2A, and Voices38. In short, the ESA is seeking some kind of restitution for the harm that "superfake" retro consoles pose to the gaming industry…

title: WoW: Forever Has A Streamer Problem
description: World of Warcraft: Forever isn't out yet, but it's already clear it has a major problem. It isn't anything in the game itself. It's not the addition of Skyborne elves that require players to pay $30, or controversial class changes like Warrior's Rage normalization. The WoW Classic community is a passionate bunch, and so there's a huge variety of strong opinions on everything related to the latest version of developer Blizzard's old-school MMORPG. That's all par for the course. Instead, it's a problem that's largely out of the community's control: streamers. Streamers have been a big part of WoW since Twitch's earliest days. The release of WoW Classic back in 2019 in particular was a watershed moment, with 1.1 million concurrent viewers and 55 million hours watched during launch week. WoW: Forever's beta isn't quite hitting those numbers so far, but considering it's not even officially out yet, interest and viewership is high. The game has a strong streamer community, and they've taken to hitting Forever's beta extremely hard, pushing it to its limits. Blizzard employees have commented multiple times that Forever's beta is breaking records. Having streamers and their communities do such robust beta testing on Forever is great, ensuring the game's full launch on November 4 will be smoother for everyone involved. Unfortunately, it hasn't taken long for the negative costs of the game's popularity with streamers to become obvious. Some streamers are already using their large communities in the Forever beta to gain an advantage over average players, whether it's members of their community donating materials so they can speedrun professions or straight-up gifting them huge amounts of gold. A streamer even went so far to promote illegal gold buying live on stream, encouraging their community to "swipe their credit card" so that they could in turn profit. Another streamer is building an in-game community so large that many worry it will swallow one server in particular…

title: My Most-Anticipated Game Was Delayed, But Its New Demo Has Proven A Fantastic Consolation
description: Originally slated for this year, At Fate's End has been delayed to 2027. And while I'm bummed that the next game from Spiritfarer studio Thunder Lotus is now months (maybe even a year) away, the new Steam demo that dropped alongside the delay announcement has been an excellent consolation prize. Having finished the one-hour slice of the upcoming action-adventure, I'm more convinced than ever that this game would have been a serious contender for everyone's Best Of lists this year had it managed to stick to its original release window. Like Spiritfarer, At Fate's End appears to combine an engrossing gameplay loop with an emotionally devastating story. However, unlike Spiritfarer, At Fate's End isn't delving into death positivity and the oftentimes messy emotions of grief, vulnerability, and forgiveness tied to the loss of a loved one (on first glance anyway--I suppose it could always touch on these). Instead, the game tells the story of how a family's fracturing loyalties can cause members to turn on one another, why the long-ignored traumas between parents and their children can linger and continue to hurt long after a parent dies, and what it takes for siblings to reopen old wounds and unearth buried insecurities so that their relationships can heal correctly and find a healthier path forward. I'm convinced this game is going to emotionally destroy me even more than Spiritfarer did, and I simply cannot wait for it to do so. In At Fate's End, you play as Shan Hemlock, the youngest and most inexperienced knight in a family of warriors. Chosen by her mother to be the next princess of blades just before the queen's death, Shan has returned to her family's home to set out across the various kingdoms ruled by her siblings to take away their swords, the source of each of their magical abilities, in order to become the next ruling monarch. These duels see Shan cross swords with her siblings in real-time action-platforming combat, but each phase of the fight is marked by…

title: Ex-Overwatch Director Jeff Kaplan Says He Never Wanted The Spotlight, But The Game Needed A Face
description: Being the face of a video game is a demanding role, as the people who step into these positions involved in these roles often find themselves on the receiving end of a lot of toxicity. Former Overwatch game director Jeff Kaplan knows this all too well, as he promoted the hero shooter for several years and regularly interacted with its fans--albeit at a "personal cost." After leaving Blizzard Entertainment in 2021, Kaplan has been quietly working on The Legend of California, the in-development game at his new studio, Kintsugiyama. Reflecting on his time as the face of Overwatch, Kaplan spoke to GameSpot about how Overwatch needed someone to fill that role. For Kaplan, this was part of Overwatch's growth and continued existence, and he felt it was needed at the time. "This is going to sound ridiculous, but I'm not someone who likes attention," Kaplan said of his time in the public-facing position. "I'm not much of an extrovert. I don't have a heavy social media presence. And so, a lot of me putting myself out there when I was at Blizzard was sort of to serve my game and my team--doing a job and a role." Overwatch--and Blizzard as a whole--has had tremendous highs and lows over the years. During periods of content droughts or Hero changes, players would often target Kaplan and other developers on the game with verbal abuse and threats. There has never been a silver bullet to eliminate player toxicity, but Blizzard discovered that dropping a ton of content into Overwatch helped change player sentiment. Overwatch added all 10 of these heroes throughout 2026. While his departure from Blizzard back in 2021 wasn't easy, Kaplan said that being freed of the responsibility of being associated with Overwatch and fading into the background turned out to be "pretty great" in the end. "There were a lot of emotions mixed up in leaving Blizzard, but one of the things that was sort of much needed for me, on a personal level, was that withdrawal," Kaplan said. "To stop reading the…

title: Jeff Kaplan Says Separation From Overwatch Was “Clinical”: ” I Never Go Back”
description: Jeff Kaplan, Overwatch's former director, said he's not played the game he was the public face of since April 2021, when he left developer Blizzard after nearly 20 years to go indie. He called his relationship with Blizzard's shooter one of "clinical separation." Kaplan revealed this to GameSpot in an interview that dove into his history with Blizzard and the creation of his new game, The Legend of California. When asked if he had continued to play Overwatch or kept tabs on it in the wake of it dropping the "2" from its name and its addition of 10 new heroes over the course of the year, Kaplan said he hadn't. He said he's essentially cut all ties with the game he used to direct. "With Overwatch, I had a very almost clinical separation, knowing how the WoW thing had gone," Kaplan said. "I've literally not played the game since April 2021." He continued: "I don't, for my own psyche, I don't read the subreddits. After I said my goodbye to competitive Overwatch and the Overwatch subreddit, I never go back and read. I don't watch YouTube [videos]. I don't search for my name in Overwatch. I don't search for Overwatch. I sort of just disconnect. I actually tell all the algorithms like, 'Yeah, I'm not really interested in Overwatch anymore. I know you think I'm the Overwatch guy, but like, that's just not for me anymore.'" It was a lesson Kaplan learned when he left the World of Warcraft team in 2008 after working on Blizzard's MMORPG for six years. He said it was more painful to step away from WoW than it was for Overwatch. "Oddly, leaving WoW was a training moment for me," he said. "When I left WoW to work on Titan [the game that would eventually become Overwatch], it was, I think, November or December of 2008. And WoW was who I was at that point. I worked every minute--every waking minute--on WoW. If I wasn't working on WoW, I was playing WoW. And every time I played WoW, I had this notepad next to the desk that I'd be filling out to walk in the next morning and go,…

title: Jeff Kaplan Was An Industry Icon, Now Peers Ignore His Emails: Ex-Overwatch Director Talks “Humbling” Reality Of Indie Dev
description: "Have you ever seen Napoleon Dynamite?" I'll admit it: When I sat down with former Blizzard developer Jeff Kaplan to discuss his legacy and what comes next, I hadn't anticipated being asked questions myself--especially ones pertaining to one of the early aughts' most iconic (and absurd) comedy films. Yet it took only 20 minutes until we reached this point--when discussing the tragedy of Uncle Rico felt like a both a natural and important conversation to have. Despite being a self-proclaimed introvert, it's easy to see how the World of Warcraft developer went on to become not just the director of Overwatch, but the highly public face of the game. There is an openness to Kaplan that fosters trust--a warmth that makes conversation feel natural. This quality was most assuredly what Blizzard was looking for as it readied itself to launch a new tentpole title that needed to make World of Warcraft-type money. From Overwatch's reveal in 2014 to Spring 2021, Kaplan was all but synonymous with the hero shooter, personally delivering showcases, press conferences, and developer updates to its massive playerbase. But despite this--and a nearly two-decade-long career at Blizzard--Kaplan ultimately chose to leave the company after demoralizing corporate interference. As such, Kaplan's new studio, Kintsugiyama, is founded on one core belief: Game developers should be the ones making game-related decisions. For the past few years, Kaplan has kept his head down in a self-imposed hermitage, his focus solely on developing Kintsugiyama's debut title, The Legend of California. From building server networks out of his dining room to getting ignored by industry contacts who once clamored for his attention, the transition from AAA legend to independent studio head has been "humbling," according to Kaplan. Yet, stripping away the corporate apparatus has only sharpened his drive to prove that great games are built by passionate developers, not corporations. The Legend of California.…
